question: What is the main goal of community mobilisation in health care?

options.A: Replacing traditional healers with foreign nurses
options.B: Building more hospitals in urban centres
options.C: Bringing people together to take joint action for health
options.D: Training only doctors to run local clinics

explanation: Community mobilisation is fundamentally about uniting individuals and groups to tackle common health issues together. [learn more](GNS124_U4_T2#GNS124_U4_T2_h1)

question: How does community mobilisation change the traditional role of patients?

options.A: It turns passive receivers of care into active partners
options.B: It forces patients to pay higher hospital bills
options.C: It stops patients from visiting doctors entirely
options.D: It requires patients to study nursing in school

explanation: Instead of just waiting for instructions, community members work alongside health workers to plan and execute health solutions. [learn more](GNS124_U4_T2#GNS124_U4_T2_h1)

question: Which of the following is a primary objective of community mobilisation?

options.A: Closing down local primary health centers
options.B: Reducing the number of working nurses
options.C: Empowering local populations to demand better services
options.D: Increasing government taxes for medical supplies

explanation: Empowerment helps community members gain the confidence and voice needed to advocate for their own health rights. [learn more](GNS124_U4_T2#GNS124_U4_T2_h2)

question: A rural village uses its own communal labor and local materials to build a shade structure for an immunization clinic. Which objective does this best demonstrate?
explanation: Using local labour and materials to support a health project is a clear example of resource mobilisation from within the community. [learn more](GNS124_U4_T2#GNS124_U4_T2_h2)

question: What does the principle of equity mean in community mobilisation?

options.A: Treating only the village elders during an outbreak
options.B: Fair distribution of health benefits without discrimination
options.C: Building clinics only in big cities
options.D: Giving equal amounts of money to every single adult

explanation: Equity ensures that all members of the community, regardless of status, have fair access to health interventions. [learn more](GNS124_U4_T2#GNS124_U4_T2_h3)

question: Why is respecting local culture vital during a community health campaign?

options.A: It prevents nurses from learning any new languages
options.B: It ensures that western medicine is completely ignored
options.C: It builds trust and encourages people to accept the health message
options.D: It allows the nurse to change the local religious practices

explanation: When health workers honor local customs and beliefs, community members feel respected and are much more likely to cooperate. [learn more](GNS124_U4_T2#GNS124_U4_T2_h3)

question: Who are considered key stakeholders in community mobilisation?

options.C: Patients admitted to distant urban hospitals
options.D: Only foreign aid workers from abroad

explanation: Traditional and religious leaders are influential figures who help guide community opinions and behaviours. [learn more](GNS124_U4_T2#GNS124_U4_T2_h4)

question: Why is it important to involve local leaders early in a health intervention?

options.A: Their endorsement helps build community trust and cooperation
options.B: It stops ordinary citizens from asking questions
options.C: They are required by law to pay for all medical equipment
options.D: They must personally diagnose every sick patient

explanation: Local populations listen closely to their leaders, making their backing crucial for high community participation. [learn more](GNS124_U4_T2#GNS124_U4_T2_h4)

question: What is the very first step in the community mobilisation process?
explanation: Before doing anything else, health workers must properly introduce themselves and gain entry through appropriate community channels. [learn more](GNS124_U4_T2#GNS124_U4_T2_h5)

question: Why is community diagnosis performed during mobilisation?

options.A: To test every resident for rare genetic disorders
options.B: To collect money from villagers for the clinic roof
options.C: To identify major local health problems and priorities together
options.D: To decide which nurses will be transferred

explanation: Community diagnosis helps health workers and residents discover what health issues matter most to the locals. [learn more](GNS124_U4_T2#GNS124_U4_T2_h5)

question: Which of the following is NOT a common challenge in community mobilisation?

options.A: Cultural resistance to new health ideas
options.C: Guaranteed 100% funding and instant community obedience
options.D: Apathy and lack of initial interest from residents

explanation: Communities are rarely instantly obedient or fully funded; engagement is usually hard work filled with resistance and roadblocks. [learn more](GNS124_U4_T2#GNS124_U4_T2_h6)

question: What happens when health workers make promises to a community and fail to keep them?

options.A: Local leaders take over nursing duties
options.B: The community becomes more eager to help
options.D: Trust is broken, leading to poor cooperation

explanation: Broken promises destroy trust, making future health initiatives extremely difficult to implement. [learn more](GNS124_U4_T2#GNS124_U4_T2_h6)

question: When does continuous monitoring of a community mobilisation project take place?

options.A: Before entering the community for the first time
options.B: Throughout the implementation of the project
options.C: Only ten years after the project has ended

explanation: Monitoring is an ongoing activity that happens while the project is running to ensure everything stays on track. [learn more](GNS124_U4_T2#GNS124_U4_T2_h7)

question: Why should community members be involved in evaluating health projects?

options.A: It stops the government from auditing the facility
options.B: It gives them the legal right to close the clinic down
options.C: It is required only for international funding bodies
options.D: It promotes accountability and shows them the results of their work

explanation: Involving locals in evaluation builds transparency and lets them see how their participation improved community health. [learn more](GNS124_U4_T2#GNS124_U4_T2_h7)
